newsitem.title: USA: Intel's position seen preserving Chips deal.
newsitem.headline: Intel's position seen preserving Chips deal.

text.p: Intel Corp's position as the world's computer chip heavyweight will likely prevent a rival bidder from interfering with its friendly $420 million takeover of Chips and Technologies Inc, arbitrageurs said.

Were it not for Intel's position and wealth, the deal would be vulnerable to an unwelcome, competing bid because of the slim premium being paid for Chips and Technologies and because the target company was not "shopped," they said.
If a new bidder did emerge, the arbs said it most likely could be Intel competitor Advanced Micro Devices Inc.
"Chips & Technologies was not shopping the company but was working closely with Intel," said Bruce LeBoss, a spokesman for Chips & Technologies.
LeBoss said he was not aware of any other interest. "(Intel chief executive) Andy Grove could put them on his credit card, but I don't see AMD doing that," LeBoss said.
Advanced Micro could not immediately be reached.

"The company was not shopped (around), which gets us mildly excited and Advanced Micro Devices is a possible buyer. The price (Intel is paying for Chips) is not that high," said an arb who declined to be named.

Early Monday, Intel said it agreed to acquire Chips and Technologies for $17.50 per share, $3.50 above Friday's Nasdaq closing price, a move that builds on the companies' joint development of computer graphics accelerators.
The accelerators speed up the display of graphics on laptops, desktop and other computers.
Under ther agreement, Intel will commence a cash tender offer for all Chips and Technologies outstanding shares at $17.50 each, Intel said.
Chips and Technologies will then merge with an Intel unit and all remaining outstanding shares of Chips and Technologies will be converted into the right to receive $17.50 per share, Intel said.
The Chips spokesman said the companies decided to merge since they were chasing the same market with the new i740 graphics chip they developed together.
A second arbitrageur, who requested anonymity, said, "I am little hard pressed to believe that if someone wanted the company, they would go up against Intel."
"There could be someone else who could pay as much as Intel, but Intel is so dominant, we are not counting on it," a third arb said.
Another arb said, "Do you think anyone wants to go up against Intel? I think it is possible, but I would not think any one would want go up against a behemoth like that."
